[plotnine](https://plotnine.org/) implements the grammar of graphics in Python.
If you know ggplot2, the layers will look familiar; most translation work is in
column mappings, pandas data preparation, argument names, and displaying plots.
This guide pairs R and Python code so you can adapt an existing R script.

The examples use the same small dataset in both languages. Run each language's
setup first, then run the examples in order. Code chunks are displayed without
execution when knitting this document, so reading it does not require a Python
installation or create exported plot files. To execute the Python snippets,
install `plotnine` and `pandas` in your Python environment:

```bash
python -m pip install plotnine pandas
```

```{r document-options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = TRUE, python.reticulate = TRUE, echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

## The translation essentials

| In R / ggplot2 | In Python / plotnine | Difference to remember |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `library(ggplot2)` | `import plotnine as p9` | Use the `p9.` prefix for plotnine functions. |
| `p <- ggplot(...)` | `p = p9.ggplot(...)` | Assignment uses `=`. |
| `aes(x, y, colour = group)` | `p9.aes("x", "y", color="group")` | Column names are strings; `color` is used throughout these examples. |
| `geom_point(colour = "red")` | `p9.geom_point(color="red")` | Constants go outside `aes()` in both languages. |
| `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `NULL` | `True`, `False`, `None` | Python spelling and capitalization differ. |
| `c(1, 2)` | `[1, 2]` or `(1, 2)` | Lists and tuples replace many uses of R vectors. |
| `c(A = "red", B = "blue")` | `{"A": "red", "B": "blue"}` | Named scale values become a dictionary. |
| `na.rm`, `show.legend`, `inherit.aes` | `na_rm`, `show_legend`, `inherit_aes` | Many dotted argument names become underscored names. |
| `geom_line(linewidth = 1)` | `p9.geom_line(size=1)` | Current plotnine line geoms use `size`; point size also uses `size`. |
| `theme(axis.text.x = ...)` | `p9.theme(axis_text_x=...)` | Theme names use underscores. |
| `print(p)` | `p.show()` | Use `show()` explicitly in Python scripts. |
| Layers continued with `+` | Enclose the entire expression in `( ... )` | Parentheses allow Python's multiline expression syntax. |

R evaluates bare column names inside `aes()`. Plotnine evaluates column-name
strings and can also evaluate expression strings, such as `"weight / 1000"`.
R expressions such as `log10(x)` or `.data[[name]]` cannot simply be pasted into
Python. For complicated transformations, create a pandas column first; for a
variable holding a column name, use `p9.aes(x=name)`.
See the official [aesthetic mapping reference](https://plotnine.org/reference/aes.html)
and [ggplot2 mapping reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/aes.html).

## Equivalent functions

The names below are available in the [plotnine API](https://plotnine.org/reference/index.html).
A matching name is a useful starting point, but check the particular function's
arguments when porting a plot.

| ggplot2 | plotnine | Purpose / translation note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ggplot()`, `aes()` | `p9.ggplot()`, `p9.aes()` | Start a plot and map columns. |
| `geom_point()`, `geom_jitter()` | `p9.geom_point()`, `p9.geom_jitter()` | Scatter plots; specify jitter width/height for control. |
| `geom_line()`, `geom_path()` | `p9.geom_line()`, `p9.geom_path()` | Lines sorted by x versus paths in row order. |
| `geom_bar()`, `geom_col()` | `p9.geom_bar()`, `p9.geom_col()` | Count rows versus plot existing y values. |
| `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()` | `p9.geom_histogram()`, `p9.geom_density()` | Binned counts versus density estimates. |
| `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_violin()` | `p9.geom_boxplot()`, `p9.geom_violin()` | Compare distributions across categories. |
| `geom_errorbar()`, `geom_ribbon()` | `p9.geom_errorbar()`, `p9.geom_ribbon()` | Map `ymin`/`ymax` as strings in Python. |
| `geom_text()`, `geom_label()`, `annotate()` | `p9.geom_text()`, `p9.geom_label()`, `p9.annotate()` | Data labels or fixed annotations. |
| `geom_smooth()` | `p9.geom_smooth()` | Specify the smoothing method explicitly. |
| `stat_summary()`, `after_stat()` | `p9.stat_summary()`, `p9.after_stat()` | Summary statistics and computed mappings. |
| `position_dodge()`, `position_jitter()` | `p9.position_dodge()`, `p9.position_jitter()` | Adjust overlapping marks. |
| `facet_wrap(~group)` | `p9.facet_wrap("group")` | Python uses a column-name string. |
| `facet_grid(group ~ year)` | `p9.facet_grid(rows="group", cols="year")` | Explicit row and column arguments. |
| `scale_colour_manual()`, `scale_fill_manual()` | `p9.scale_color_manual()`, `p9.scale_fill_manual()` | Named palettes use dictionaries. |
| `scale_x_log10()`, `scale_y_log10()` | `p9.scale_x_log10()`, `p9.scale_y_log10()` | Log axes; data must suit the transformation. |
| `scale_x_continuous()`, `scale_y_discrete()` | `p9.scale_x_continuous()`, `p9.scale_y_discrete()` | Set breaks, labels, and limits. |
| `coord_cartesian()`, `coord_flip()` | `p9.coord_cartesian()`, `p9.coord_flip()` | Zoom or flip axes. |
| `labs()`, `guides()`, `guide_legend()` | `p9.labs()`, `p9.guides()`, `p9.guide_legend()` | Axis titles, captions, and legend control. |
| `theme_minimal()`, `theme_bw()` | `p9.theme_minimal()`, `p9.theme_bw()` | Choose a base theme. |
| `theme()`, `element_text()`, `element_blank()` | `p9.theme()`, `p9.element_text()`, `p9.element_blank()` | Theme properties and text alignment differ. |
| `ggsave(..., plot = p)` | `p.save(...)` | Save the specified plot object. |
| `pdf(); print(p1); print(p2); dev.off()` | `p9.save_as_pdf_pages([p1, p2], ...)` | Export one plot per PDF page. |

## Shared example data

### R setup

```{r r-setup}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

df <- data.frame(
  subject = rep(1:4, each = 3),
  group = rep(c("control", "control", "treated", "treated"), each = 3),
  day = rep(c(0, 7, 14), times = 4),
  value = c(10, 12, 14, 11, 13, 15, 10, 15, 20, 12, 17, 22)
)
df$group <- factor(df$group, levels = c("control", "treated"))
palette <- c(control = "#0072B2", treated = "#D55E00")
```

### Python setup

```{r}
library(reticulate)
# Use a specific Python environment if needed
# use_python("/path/to/python", required = TRUE)
use_python("/mnt/windows/Program/ubuntu/pyenv/versions/3.13.9/bin/python", required = TRUE)
```

```{python python-setup}
import pandas as pd
import plotnine as p9

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "subject": [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4],
    "group": ["control"] * 6 + ["treated"] * 6,
    "day": [0, 7, 14] * 4,
    "value": [10, 12, 14, 11, 13, 15, 10, 15, 20, 12, 17, 22],
})
df["group"] = pd.Categorical(
    df["group"], categories=["control", "treated"], ordered=True
)
palette = {"control": "#0072B2", "treated": "#D55E00"}
```

R factors translate to pandas categorical columns. Numeric codes do not become
categories automatically: mapping a numeric `subject` to color would normally
produce a continuous scale. Convert it to a categorical column when you want
four distinct colors. Set category order explicitly to control axes, legends,
and facets rather than relying on the order strings happen to appear.

## Paired examples

### Scatter plot: mapping versus setting

```{r scatter-r}
p_scatter <- ggplot(df, aes(day, value, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = palette) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "Response", colour = "Group") +
  theme_minimal()
print(p_scatter)
```

```{python scatter-python}
p_scatter = (
    p9.ggplot(df, p9.aes("day", "value", color="group"))
    + p9.geom_point(size=3, alpha=0.8)
    + p9.scale_color_manual(values=palette)
    + p9.labs(x="Day", y="Response", color="Group")
    + p9.theme_minimal()
)
p_scatter.show()
```

Both plots show response against day, with a legend distinguishing the groups.
`p9.aes(color="group")` maps a column; `p9.geom_point(color="red")` sets every
point to red without a color legend. `p9.aes(color="red")` instead asks plotnine
to evaluate `red`, typically causing an error when that column does not exist.

### Repeated measurements: group lines by subject

```{r lines-r}
p_lines <- ggplot(df, aes(day, value, colour = group, group = subject)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = palette)
print(p_lines)
```

```{python lines-python}
p_lines = (
    p9.ggplot(df, p9.aes("day", "value", color="group", group="subject"))
    + p9.geom_line(size=0.8)
    + p9.geom_point(size=2)
    + p9.scale_color_manual(values=palette)
)
p_lines.show()
```

There should be four trajectories, with two subjects sharing each group color.
Without `group="subject"`, the discrete color mapping groups by treatment and
can connect different subjects. `geom_line()` orders by x within each group;
`geom_path()` follows row order. For a single trajectory on a discrete x axis,
`aes(group=1)` can be necessary in both languages.
Modern ggplot2 uses `linewidth` for line thickness; plotnine's
[geom_line reference](https://plotnine.org/reference/geom_line.html) uses `size`.

### Bars: row counts versus precomputed values

Count observations in each group (six rows each):

```{r counts-r}
ggplot(df, aes(group, fill = group)) +
  geom_bar() + scale_fill_manual(values = palette)
```

```{python counts-python}
p_counts = (
    p9.ggplot(df, p9.aes("group", fill="group"))
    + p9.geom_bar()
    + p9.scale_fill_manual(values=palette)
)
p_counts.show()
```

For means by group and day, summarize first and use `geom_col()`. Here
`geom_bar()` would count summary rows instead of displaying their means.

```{r summary-r}
summary_df <- df |>
  group_by(group, day) |>
  summarise(mean_value = mean(value), .groups = "drop")

p_bars <- ggplot(summary_df, aes(factor(day), mean_value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "Mean response")
print(p_bars)
```

```{python summary-python}
summary_df = (
    df.groupby(["group", "day"], observed=True, as_index=False)
    .agg(mean_value=("value", "mean"))
)
p_bars = (
    p9.ggplot(summary_df, p9.aes("factor(day)", "mean_value", fill="group"))
    + p9.geom_col(position=p9.position_dodge(width=0.8), width=0.7)
    + p9.scale_fill_manual(values=palette)
    + p9.labs(x="Day", y="Mean response")
)
p_bars.show()
```

Control means are 10.5, 12.5, and 14.5; treated means are 11, 16, and 21.
`as_index=False` keeps grouping keys as columns that plotnine can map.
`observed=True` limits categorical grouping to observed combinations.
`"factor(day)"` is a supported plotnine expression that gives equally spaced,
discrete day labels; map `"day"` to preserve a numeric time axis.

### Histogram: computed density and explicit bins

```{r histogram-r}
ggplot(df, aes(value, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, boundary = 0, fill = "grey70", colour = "white")
```

```{python histogram-python}
p_hist = (
    p9.ggplot(df, p9.aes("value", y=p9.after_stat("density")))
    + p9.geom_histogram(binwidth=2, boundary=0, fill="#B3B3B3", color="white")
)
p_hist.show()
```

The density is calculated by the binning statistic, so it is not a column in
`df`. R uses `after_stat(density)`; Python uses `p9.after_stat("density")`.
Specify bin width and boundary to make bin placement comparable. R color names such as `"grey70"` are not all recognized in Python;
use a hex color such as `"#B3B3B3"` for portability. Matching code still need
not produce identical fonts, spacing, or rendered pixels.

### Facets and explicit smoothing

```{r facets-r}
p_facets <- ggplot(df, aes(day, value)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~group, ncol = 2)
print(p_facets)
```

```{python facets-python}
p_facets = (
    p9.ggplot(df, p9.aes("day", "value"))
    + p9.geom_point()
    + p9.geom_smooth(method="lm", formula="y ~ x", se=False)
    + p9.facet_wrap("group", ncol=2)
)
p_facets.show()
```

Each panel shows one group's observations and fitted linear trend.
R facet formulas become column strings; for two variables, use
`p9.facet_grid(rows="group", cols="day")`.
`scales="free_y"` lets panels have different y ranges but makes visual
comparisons less direct. See [facet_grid](https://plotnine.org/reference/facet_grid.html).

Smoother defaults and implementations can differ between R and Python. Choose
`method="lm"` explicitly for this example. The formula is a string in Python,
and its `x`/`y` refer to mapped aesthetics. Plotnine's `loess` method requires
`scikit-misc`; see [stat_smooth](https://plotnine.org/reference/stat_smooth.html).

### Themes, labels, annotations, and zoom

```{r theme-r}
p_styled <- p_scatter +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y = 21, label = "Follow-up", size = 4) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(9, 23)) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
print(p_styled)
```

```{python theme-python}
p_styled = (
    p_scatter
    + p9.annotate("text", x=7, y=21, label="Follow-up", size=10)
    + p9.coord_cartesian(ylim=(9, 23))
    + p9.theme(
        axis_text_x=p9.element_text(angle=45, ha="right"),
        legend_position="bottom",
        panel_grid_minor=p9.element_blank(),
        figure_size=(7, 4),
    )
)
p_styled.show()
```

Translate dotted theme names to underscores. Plotnine text alignment uses
`ha="right"`/`va="top"`, where R commonly uses numeric `hjust`/`vjust`.
Text geom sizes use different units (ggplot2's default is mm; plotnine uses
points), so the annotation sizes above are approximate visual equivalents.
See [element_text](https://plotnine.org/reference/element_text.html).

`coord_cartesian(ylim=...)` zooms the display while retaining data for
statistics. Scale limits, such as `scale_y_continuous(limits=...)`, can remove
observations before a summary or smoother is computed. This distinction
matters in both languages.

### Save an image or a multipage PDF

Run these snippets only when you want to write files to the working directory.

```{r save-r}
ggsave("scatter-r.png", plot = p_scatter, width = 7, height = 4,
       units = "in", dpi = 300)
pdf("plots-r.pdf", width = 7, height = 4)
print(p_scatter)
print(p_bars)
dev.off()
```

```{python save-python}
p_scatter.save("scatter-python.png", width=7, height=4, units="in", dpi=300)
p9.save_as_pdf_pages(
    [p_scatter + p9.theme(figure_size=(7, 4)),
     p_bars + p9.theme(figure_size=(7, 4))],
    filename="plots-python.pdf",
)
```

Use the plot object's [save method](https://plotnine.org/reference/ggplot.html)
in place of `ggsave()`. `figure_size` is a `(width, height)` tuple in inches.
`save_as_pdf_pages()` writes one plot per page; setting each plot's theme lets
you control each page's size.

## Data preparation: translating tidyverse code

Plotnine handles plotting; pandas handles most transformations you previously
performed with dplyr or tidyr.

| R | Python / pandas | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `filter(df, day > 0)` | `df.loc[df["day"] > 0].copy()` | Boolean mask selects rows; copy before modifying the subset. |
| `select(df, day, value)` | `df[["day", "value"]]` | A list of names selects multiple columns. |
| `mutate(df, doubled = value * 2)` | `df.assign(doubled=df["value"] * 2)` | Returns a new frame with the new column. |
| `arrange(df, subject, day)` | `df.sort_values(["subject", "day"])` | Important for row-order geoms such as paths. |
| `group_by(...) |> summarise(...)` | `df.groupby(..., as_index=False).agg(...)` | Keep grouping columns out of the index for plotting. |
| `drop_na(df, value)` | `df.dropna(subset=["value"])` | Explicitly remove missing plotting values. |
| `factor(x, levels = ...)` | `pd.Categorical(x, categories=..., ordered=True)` | Specify levels and order. |
| `pivot_longer(...)` | `df.melt(...)` | Convert measurements in separate columns to long form. |

For example, combine two measurement columns into one value column and a
measurement label that can be mapped to color or used for facets:

```{r reshape-r}
wide <- data.frame(day = c(0, 7, 14), marker_a = c(10, 12, 14),
                   marker_b = c(11, 16, 21))
long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(marker_a, marker_b),
                     names_to = "marker", values_to = "value")
ggplot(long, aes(day, value, colour = marker)) + geom_line()
```

```{python reshape-python}
wide = pd.DataFrame({
    "day": [0, 7, 14], "marker_a": [10, 12, 14], "marker_b": [11, 16, 21]
})
long = wide.melt(
    id_vars="day", value_vars=["marker_a", "marker_b"],
    var_name="marker", value_name="value",
)
p_long = (
    p9.ggplot(long, p9.aes("day", "value", color="marker"))
    + p9.geom_line()
)
p_long.show()
```

For compound filters, use parentheses around each pandas condition:
`df.loc[(df["day"] > 0) & (df["group"] == "treated")]`.
Python `and`/`or` do not combine pandas boolean Series; use `&`/`|`.
Pandas means skip missing values by default, whereas R's `mean()` needs
`na.rm=TRUE` to do so. Make your missing-data policy explicit when comparing
summaries across languages.

## Common translation problems

| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| A column cannot be found | Use `aes("day", "value")`; confirm spelling and that grouping keys remain columns. Rename awkward column names before using expressions. |
| A continuous legend appears for category codes | Convert the numeric column to a pandas categorical before mapping it. |
| Lines join unrelated observations | Set `group` to the subject or series identifier. |
| Bars display counts instead of means | Use `geom_col()` with the prepared y column. |
| Python rejects a multiline plot | Wrap the full `ggplot(...) + ...` expression in parentheses. |
| Python rejects `linewidth` or a dotted keyword | Check the geom reference; use `size` for these line examples and underscored argument names. |
| A script runs but no plot appears | Call `p.show()` or save the plot explicitly. |
| A smoother changes after applying limits | Use coordinate zoom if you want statistics based on the full data. |
| An R extension function is unavailable | ggplot2 extensions do not transfer automatically; find a Python implementation or reconstruct the layer from prepared data. |

When adapting a larger R plot, translate data preparation first, add one layer
at a time, and compare grouping, category order, summaries, and axis ranges
before tuning its appearance. Record package versions for reproducible work:
`packageVersion("ggplot2")` in R, and `p9.__version__` / `pd.__version__` in Python.


```{r python-info, include=FALSE}
# This will print the active Python path, version, and loaded packages
reticulate::py_config()
```
